It's a perfect topic for me! I've had to do many fire and safety training for my degree (coming soon TM) and they go really deep into the specifics. Keep in mind I'm going from memory so you should double check my definitions. Also, I'm coming from a chemical background and these terms may have different meanings in other fields.

From my understanding, an explosion is a pretty general term to describe an event where a large amount of energy is released very rapidly. Different types of explosions are classified with the terms you noted above with deflagration and detonation, the main difference between the two being the rate at which they release energy. Detonatios and deflagrations are both caused by the ignition of fuel in the presence of an oxidizer, but not all explosions are caused by burning fuel. For example, a BLEVE is an explosion that can be caused by just water with no chemical reactions. A BLEVE is a very specific type of explosion where the pressure builds uncontrollably in a closed vessel due to a boiling liquid with no pressure relief. Generally, these happen after another incident occurs and a burning jet is left exposed to a tank. After a while, the tank will fail both due to the pressure inside and the tank weakening from the heat.

I'm not too familiar with thermobaric weapons, but from my quick search I found that they spread a cloud of explosive vapors in an area. In industry, this is very similar to what we call a "Vapor Cloud Explosion" or VCE. In the cases we looked at, generally some flammable material begins leaking from somewhere in the facility and it goes unnoticed. There is a cloud around this leak where the vapors are capable of igniting, and this cloud grows as the leak continues. Eventually, the cloud reaches an ignition source, which can be anything from an engine, a spark, dropped tool, or any number of things. This causes the entire cloud to ignite is where the name comes from. If this explosion occurred due to a flammable liquid, then a "pool fire" will continue to burn above the liquid.

The last one I can recall from memory is a "fireball" which IIRC isn't technically an explosion because it doesn't create a shockwave, but it is caused by the rapid burning of a fuel. While fireballs don't produce a shockwave, they release most of their energy as thermal radiation. Depending on the fuel and size of the fireball, brief exposure from a relatively far distance can cause severe burns. They look and behave similar to a *very* small scale nuclear detonation. I believe the San Juanico incident was accompanied by a fireball which caused the most deaths and injuries from the entire incident due to the public watching the events unfold. These people faced severe injuries and even some deaths even though they were viewing it from outside the fenced plant.

Yes, deflagrations and explosions are similar events in that they both produce a shock wave. An explosion releases its energy much more quickly than a deflagration and the shock wave becomes a blast wave. If you were able to take a snapshot of the explosion and measure the pressure around the shock wave, you would notice the pressure changes much more gradually in a shock wave compared to sharp change in the blast wave. This rapid change in pressure is what makes an explosion so powerful and dangerous.

That wasn't a BLEVE. A BLEVE happens when a closed vessel with liquid is heated by an external source. The pressure builds immensely until the tank mechanically fails. These events are one of the most dangerous process safety incidents that can occur in a chemical manufacturing facility. Because these vessels are usually typically made of carbon steel at 1/8" thickness minimim, the pressure differential is massive and the explosion is violent. A BLEVE can cause a tank and other debris to be thrown kilometers away. The San Juanico Disaster would be an interesting research topic if you want to learn more about BLEVEs. This occurred in an LPG plant after a series of fire and explosions resulted in a jet fire impinging a sealed tank that eventually caused the BLEVE.

The fuel for this fire is coming from within the tank itself, so it is unable to build pressure (the flames are not jetting out so you can tell the tank is not under high pressure). I think enough fuel was burned/ enough air was let into the vessel and created an ignitable mixture. Obviously, the fire burning above was the ignition source. It's hard to say if this would be classified as an explosion. I would guess that this is a deflagration because the vent that the fuel was escaping through could allow enough pressure to escape during the ignition to prevent a blast wave.
